prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full round-1 exchange I still place B006 alone as the prize. The scientific case is not in dispute among us: Holst's human incretin physiology, Drucker's receptor biology and tissue actions, and the albumin-binding acylation that gave liraglutide and semaglutide durable action form one chain, now validated by large randomized trials in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Physiology or Medicine has a long record of recognising work that turned a defined mechanism into a medicine, and this is a mature, independently replicated case. The question that remains is which third name best represents the chain. I hold that Knudsen does, because without her step the physiology would not have become a drug class. The citation should state both parts openly, physiology and development into long-acting therapy, so that nobody can read it as honouring either one alone.
statement.case_against: The weaknesses are real and I do not think they can be argued away. First, the three-person cap leaves out Habener and other early contributors to the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, and Mojsov's own priority claim is contested; omitting her will be criticised. Second, crediting an industrial design step invites the objection that the prize drifts toward pharmaceutical development, and the committee would then have to apply the same standard to B004 and B040. Third, the clinical field is still moving, with new agents, long-term safety data and outcomes beyond metabolism still accumulating, so later chapters are not settled. Neither trio is clean; mine is the one I find easier to defend on documented, consequential contribution.

responses.point: Svenningsson moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, arguing that a Physiology or Medicine prize should centre on the hormone's biology and active molecular form, with industrial analogue engineering acknowledged in the citation.
responses.response: I take this argument seriously, since it was my own concern in opening about the three kinds of work under one heading. Where I differ is that a citation can acknowledge engineering without crediting it, but a prize whose stated rationale is the therapy cannot honestly leave out the person whose work produced the therapy. Acknowledgement in wording is also weaker than a name. I also find the discovery-versus-optimisation line hard to hold, because the acylation was a mechanistic insight about half-life and albumin binding, not only routine optimisation. I have not changed my configuration, but your argument is the strongest one against it.

responses.point: Perlmann credits Mojsov for identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) form, omits Knudsen, and asks how the citation should be worded to reflect that choice. Perlmann also notes a second part such as the UPR would force removal of a GLP-1 laureate.
responses.response: Your trio has a coherent logic, but I cannot see how it settles the priority question you yourself raise. Mojsov's priority is contested and Habener is outside the supplied names, so a citation that names the active form but omits Habener makes the peptide-identification chapter harder to defend than the acylation chapter, where the contribution is well documented. On a second part, I agree with your own conclusion that pairing B039 with B006 would require trimming B006 to two names and dropping the translational part. I would not trade that away, so I keep B039 outside my configuration even though its credit is clean.

responses.point: El-Manira supports Drucker, Holst and Knudsen and says the committee should state its translation principle openly because it bears on B004 and B040. He has not resolved whether physiology, peptide chemistry and drug engineering form one achievement or several.
responses.response: I agree that the principle must be stated and applied consistently. My answer is that translation can be credited when it is itself a mechanism-based invention that defines the therapeutic class and is independently shown to change outcomes, which is the case for acylated analogues. I would apply the same test to B004 and B040, and I think B004 fails mainly on attribution rather than on principle, because Eshhar sits outside the names and the Rosenberg line is a different achievement. On your question of one achievement or several, I treat B006 as one achievement, the incretin axis from physiology to therapy, and I think the citation wording should say so.

responses.point: Linnarsson names Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, wants a physiology-centred prize, and warns that if drug development is inseparable from benefit to humankind a physiology-only trio would be too academic.
responses.response: Your own caveat is close to my view. If the benefit to humankind is part of what the committee is rewarding, and the randomized outcome trials make it so, then a physiology-only trio is exactly the too-academic outcome you describe. On the Habener question we agree that it cannot be settled from these files. That uncertainty is a reason to avoid resting the third place on the contested priority claim. I also still hold that cGAS-STING deserves a higher place than it received among immunology candidates, but as an alternative and not as a second part, since its translation is not established.

responses.point: Sandberg would accept swapping Mojsov for Knudsen if the citation named the therapeutic achievement.
responses.response: That conditional is the basis on which I would ask the committee to agree. The two configurations differ only in the third name and in the citation, so our real disagreement is narrow. I would propose the wording 'physiology of GLP-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies' because it names the physiology and the therapy, and it states the translation principle without extending it beyond what is documented. I would accept a sentence in the committee's motivation noting that the identification of the active peptide involved other contributors, including Habener and Mojsov.

uncertainties: The Mojsov and Habener priority record for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is not settled by the supplied files, and I rely on recollection, not primary documents.
Whether crediting Knudsen is consistent with how the committee will treat translation in B004 and B040, and whether the majority sees acylation as discovery or as development.
Whether a second part (B004, B028 or B039) is justified, given that B006 already uses three names, and I would not drop a B006 name to make room.
Whether long-term safety data and outcomes beyond metabolism will change the assessment of the later chapters of the story.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. I have no documented personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. B028 and the autoimmunity candidates are near my field, but I do not infer a connection from shared topics, and I would follow the shared protocol if one were documented.
